=== REQUIREMENTS.md ===
# Mine

Mine is a set of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) to digitalize once personal or professional life.
The key idea is to save everything in a repo as markdown files. This can be calendar entries, diaries, markdowns extracted from voice recordings / pdfs / .. These .md files can easily be ported to new apps without a vendor lock-in are processed via an (AI) assistant to help you plan your day, keep track of tasks, remind you of memories a.k.a. a second brain.
To keep complexity to a minimum each use-case will have a separate folder. e.g. the calender PWA lives completely in a 'calendar' folder as does the zettelkasten and all the other apps. Each folder contains a 'sample' folder with samples how the markdowns shall look and a REQUIREMENTS.md to describe how the PWA works.

## Main PWA

The main app is a PWA in the root directory with tiles to call the other apps.
Each tile has the apps folder name at the bottom and the respective icon.svg above it.

### PWA Setup & GitHub Sync

#### Initialization (first run)
- User opens the main app URL (GitHub Pages) on the phone.
- User installs it via "Add to Home Screen" (iOS: Safari → Share; Android: Chrome menu).
- On first launch, the app shows a setup screen asking for:
  - GitHub owner, data repo, and branch
  - Fine-grained personal access token (only this repo, "Contents: read and write", with expiry)
- App checks the connection with a test request (GET repo); on failure it shows a clear error.
- Settings and token are stored locally (IndexedDB); the token is never logged or displayed.
- Service worker caches the app shell so the app opens offline.
- App loads the file list with SHAs via the Git Trees API (recursive) and fetches all
  Markdown files into the local cache.

### Sending data to GitHub
- User creates, edits, or moves an item (e.g. Kanban card to "Doing").
- Change is written to the local cache immediately (UI updates instantly) and added
  to a sync queue.
- Sync worker processes the queue in order:
  - Create/update: PUT to the Contents API with the file content in Base64
    (UTF-8 safe, so umlauts work), a commit message, and the current SHA for updates.
  - Delete: DELETE to the Contents API with SHA and commit message.
- On success: store the new SHA returned by GitHub and remove the item from the queue.
- On conflict (409/422, file changed elsewhere): reload the file, keep the remote
  version, notify the user, and never overwrite silently.
- On 401/403: pause sync and link the user to settings to renew the token.
- Offline: the queue persists; sync runs automatically when the app regains
  connectivity or is reopened.
- A sync indicator shows: in sync / pending / error.

# Calendar
 # Calendar

Calendar is a plugin to manage your calendar.

Features

## UI
- The UI consists of a navigation pane at the top and a big calendar window on the rest of the window.
- In the top pane are these widgets from left to right:
  - left/right button to move to the previous/next day/week/month/year (depending on current view)
  - the current day/week/month/year with a small downward arrow to indicate a dropdown. When clicked a calendar month view is show with all days in this dropdown view. The month is shown on the top left and on the top right is a left/right arrow to go to the previous/next month.  When the user clicks on the month in the extended view it switches to year. The year view has all the last 9 years (3x3).
  - A dropdown to select the view to be either day/week/month/year.
    - The year view shows all months and days. On the top of each month is a ['M','T','W','T','F','S','S'] column indicating the weekday. Each row is a new week. Current day is highlighted. The user can click on the day and a popup shows the entries on that day. If there is a calendar entry on that day the day has the background color of the entrys group. For multiple entries they are split. If a user disables a group via the group dropdown filter then it is not shown.
    - The month columns are the workdays starting from monday. Each row is a new week. When the user clicks on a day it opens a popup to create a new calendar entry.
      - The calendar entry popup has a top row to fill the title below it a button group in a row to select the type. All other field (see the sample folder) are below it. At the bottom of the popup is a 'discard' and a 'save' button.
    - The calendar entry items are show as rows per day field in the month overview, Sorted by the time they start. The 'task' items have a rectangular icon at the right to mark them done. A completed item has a done arrow in the rectangle. For a task just the date is set, not the time (which is 00:00:00 to 23:59:59 for this day)
    - The week view shows the workdays starting from monday. The rows is the time showing all 24h of the day.
    - The day view is like the week view but only for the specific day. It shows more details of the calendar entries.
  - A dropdown to filter the calendar groups (color). If a user double-clicks on the calendar group icons he can add descriptions to the colors.

content.text:
I've read `REQUIREMENTS.md`, `calendar/REQUIREMENTS.md`, both samples, and the icon. Short answers before the grilling starts:

**Is it possible?** Yes — but only if you build it a specific way. Shared token/settings works because *same origin = same storage*. `https://you.github.io/mine/` and `https://you.github.io/mine/calendar/` are the same origin (path is irrelevant to storage), so IndexedDB is shared automatically, no message passing needed.

The trap: that only holds while it's **one installed PWA**. If you install the calendar separately as its own home-screen app, iOS gives each home-screen web app its own isolated storage container — the calendar would come up with no token. (Worth verifying on your actual phone, but I'd design around it.) So "subfolders" must mean *source layout + routes inside one installable app*, not N installable apps.

**Do the REQUIREMENTS make sense?** The sync chapter is solid and realistic — Trees API for listing, Contents API with Base64 for writes, SHA tracking, queue, conflict on 409/422. That's the right shape. What's broken or missing:

1. No code-repo/data-repo split stated. Pages site must be public; your diary must not be.
2. `alert: on-start, 15` — **no browser can schedule a local notification while closed.** Notification Triggers API doesn't exist anywhere; iOS has no Background Sync either. Reminders are not implementable as written.
3. "fetches *all* Markdown files into the local cache" — fine at 500 files, not at 20k, and it couples every app to every other app's data.
4. The two calendar samples disagree with each other: `start:` vs `date:`, `done: None` vs `done: false`. `None` isn't YAML (it's a string, not null).
5. `repeat: weekly` with one-file-per-event has no answer for "skip this Tuesday" or "move just this instance" — and no `until`.
6. Filenames `20260418-1.md` give no stable identity; renaming/moving a day breaks it.
7. Conflict rule "keep the remote version, notify" = silently throwing away what the user just typed.

Starting at the root of the tree, because almost everything else hangs off it:

Good — that also means the setup screen's "owner / repo / branch" is the data repo, and the token can be scoped to a repo that contains no code.

Now the schema branch. Your two samples imply one entry = one file, but the naming (`20260418-1.md`) has a concrete multi-device failure: the counter is assigned at creation, so your phone offline and your laptop offline both mint `-2` on the same day and collide when the queue drains.

Also relevant: the Trees API gives you **every path + SHA in one request**, with no file contents. So whatever you put in the *path* is queryable for free, and anything only in the frontmatter costs a download of every file.

content.text:
Now the entry schema. Your two samples contradict each other in five places, and one of them is a real correctness bug: `date: '2026-04-18T00:00:00Z'` for the trash task is 02:00 local time in Berlin — an all-day task stored as a UTC instant lands on the wrong day for anyone not on UTC, and breaks twice a year on DST.

Other cleanups: `None` is a YAML *string*, not null (parsers give you `"None"`); `duration` is derivable from start/end; `alert` mixes a keyword and an integer in one list; `done` is meaningless on an event.

questions.question: How should the entry frontmatter be unified across event and task?

options.label: iCal-style: start/end switch type (Recommended)
options.description: One key pair for both kinds. A bare date means all-day/floating (no timezone bug); a full timestamp with Z means a real instant. This is exactly how iCalendar's DATE vs DATE-TIME works, so export to .ics later is mechanical. Absent keys replace all the 'None' values.
options.preview:
# event
title: "Project Phoenix: Weekly Sync"
type: event
start: 2026-04-18T14:00:00Z
end:   2026-04-18T15:00:00Z
group: work
location: "Conf 3B"
alerts: [0, 15]   # min before, 0=start
participants: [jane@ex.com]

# task (all-day: bare dates)
title: "take out the trash"
type: task
start: 2026-04-18
done: false
group: home
alerts: [0]

rules: omit empty keys, never "None"
       no duration (= end - start)
       done only on type: task

options.label: Explicit allDay flag
options.description: Keep start/end always as full timestamps and add `allDay: true`. More explicit to read, but redundant — and you must remember to ignore the time portion whenever allDay is set, which is the classic place this bug comes back.
options.preview:
type: task
allDay: true
start: 2026-04-18T00:00:00+02:00
end:   2026-04-18T23:59:59+02:00

2 sources of truth for one fact

options.label: Local wall time + tz field
options.description: Store what a clock on the wall said, plus the zone: `start: 2026-04-18T16:00` / `tz: Europe/Berlin`. Correct for 'my 9am standup stays 9am when I fly', but every comparison needs a tz library, and the samples' Z form is thrown away.
options.preview:
start: 2026-04-18T16:00
end:   2026-04-18T17:00
tz: Europe/Berlin

needs Intl/tz math everywhere
right answer for travel, more code

message.content: Can we rename 'repeat' to 'recurrence' and use RRULE from the iCalendar standard, RFC 5545?

content.text:
Yes — that's strictly better, and it buys more than a rename:

- `recurrence: "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA;INTERVAL=1;UNTIL=20270101T000000Z"` — `UNTIL`, `COUNT`, `INTERVAL`, `BYDAY` all come for free instead of you inventing them.
- RFC 5545 already has the exception vocabulary, so my ad-hoc `except:` becomes **`exdate:`** (skipped occurrences) and you also get **`rdate:`** (extra one-off occurrences bolted onto a series).
- `DTSTART` is just our existing `start`, so nothing new. Combined with the DATE/DATE-TIME decision we already made, `.ics` export becomes close to a direct field copy.

One cost to name: RRULE expansion is not a thing you want to hand-write — `BYSETPOS`, `BYMONTHDAY=-1`, DST-crossing weeklies are where everyone gets it wrong. That means a dependency (`rrule.js`, ~50KB, vendored as a local ESM file so there's still no build step) or restricting yourself to a documented subset the app actually parses. I'd vendor the library and support full RRULE on read, while the UI only *writes* the common cases.

Schema is now:

```yaml
start: 2026-04-18          # = DTSTART
recurrence: "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA"
exdate: [2026-05-02]       # skip these
rdate:  [2026-05-04]       # plus these
```

That still leaves the storage question open — `FREQ=WEEKLY` with no `UNTIL` renders forever, so the file can't be found by walking the month folder it was created in:

Now the read path. `REQUIREMENTS.md` says "fetches **all** Markdown files into the local cache" — I pushed back on that earlier, but having costed it out I think the clause is closer to right than my objection was. A decade of calendar entries is ~3000 files × ~500 B ≈ 1.5 MB, so mirroring is cheaper than range logic. The real problem isn't the bytes, it's that per-file fetching means ~3000 HTTP requests on first run.

Two facts that shape this: `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/tarball/{branch}` returns the whole tree in **one** request and browsers now gunzip natively via `DecompressionStream('gzip')` (tar itself is ~40 lines to walk); and `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/commits/{branch}` with `If-None-Match` returns 304 and **doesn't count against your rate limit**, so "has anything changed?" is nearly free.

content.text: Write path. One thing our own data model changed: with random-id filenames and override files, nearly every write is a **create at a fresh path**, which can't conflict. But moving an entry to another date is now a delete + create — and with the Contents API that's two separate commits, so a crash or an offline queue drain interrupted in between leaves the entry duplicated or vanished.

questions.question: Which GitHub write mechanism should the sync queue use?

options.label: Git Data API, one commit per drain (Recommended)
options.description: Build blobs, a tree and a commit, then update the ref with the expected old SHA. A whole queue drain — any number of files, creates and deletes together — lands as one atomic commit, so a move is never half-applied. Rejection means someone else pushed: re-pull and retry, which succeeds because your paths are distinct.
options.preview:
drain queue:
  POST /git/blobs      x N
  POST /git/trees      (base_tree)
  POST /git/commits
  PATCH /git/refs/heads/main
     expects old sha, no force

move = delete+create, 1 commit
4 + N requests per drain, not 2 per file
rejected -> re-pull, rebuild, retry
~80 lines more than Contents API

options.label: Contents API per file (as in REQUIREMENTS)
options.description: PUT with Base64 content and the file's SHA, DELETE with SHA. Exactly what REQUIREMENTS.md already specifies, and the simplest possible code. Cost: one commit per file, a move is two non-atomic commits, and a 20-entry offline backlog is 20 commits.

options.label: Contents API, but moves avoided by design
options.description: Keep the simple Contents API and remove the only operation that needs atomicity: make the path immutable after creation, so changing an entry's date is a frontmatter edit and the file stays in its original month folder. Cost: the path stops telling the truth about the date.

content.text:
Conflict policy. The Git Data API retry already handles "someone pushed unrelated files". The genuine conflict left is: the same entry edited on your laptop and on your phone since the last pull. Detect it by storing, with each queued change, the blob SHA it was based on, and comparing that to the remote path's blob SHA at drain time.

`REQUIREMENTS.md` currently says "keep the remote version, notify the user" — which does not overwrite silently, but does throw away what you just typed.

options.description: Remote stays at the canonical path; your version is committed next to it as a .conflict file and shown in the UI with a 'keep mine / keep theirs / keep both' prompt. Nothing is ever lost, the leftover is plain markdown readable in any editor, and the queue drains cleanly instead of jamming.

content.text:
Now the feasibility gap I flagged at the start, since the schema has `alerts: [0, 15]` and that field is currently a promise the platform can't keep.

The hard facts: there is **no** way for a web app to schedule a local notification for later — Notification Triggers was an origin trial that never shipped. Web Push works (iOS 16.4+ for installed PWAs), but it requires something *awake* at alert time to send it, and Periodic Background Sync doesn't exist in Safari. So a real reminder needs a scheduler somewhere outside your phone — which collides with "the token only ever lives on the device".

One way out that fits your architecture with no hosting at all: a **GitHub Actions cron in the private data repo**. It already has the data, it can hold VAPID keys as repo secrets, and it costs nothing. Caveat: scheduled workflows on GitHub are routinely delayed 5–20 minutes, so "15 minutes before" can arrive at 3 minutes before.

content.text:
Token security. Worth noting one thing that's *not* an option: the OAuth device flow would avoid a hand-made PAT, but GitHub's `login/device/code` endpoints send no CORS headers, so browser JS can't call them without a proxy. A fine-grained PAT is the only no-backend path.

What's left is the at-rest posture — and it has a project-wide consequence, because the real threat to a browser-held token isn't theft of your phone, it's any injected script on your origin being able to read IndexedDB.

questions.question: How is the PAT protected at rest, and what does that imply for the app?

options.label: Plaintext IndexedDB + strict CSP, zero CDNs (Recommended)
options.description: The token is as safe as your unlocked device, and the XSS route is closed off by policy instead of by encryption: a locked-down CSP and every dependency vendored into /shared/vendor/ rather than loaded from a CDN. Also tracks the token's expiry and warns before it lapses.
options.preview:
stored: {owner, repo, branch,
         token, expiresAt}
in IndexedDB, plaintext

<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-
  Policy" content="default-src
  'self'; connect-src 'self'
  https://api.github.com
  https://codeload.github.com;
  script-src 'self'">

consequence: no cdnjs, no unpkg,
  no Google Fonts - vendor all
never log or render the token
warn 14 days before expiresAt

options.label: Encrypted with a passcode
options.description: Token sealed with AES-GCM under a PBKDF2 key from a passcode you type on every cold start. Protects against someone with your unlocked phone poking at devtools. Cost: a passcode prompt before any sync, and the key sits in memory while the app runs anyway, so XSS is barely slowed.

content.text: Service worker. This is where self-hosted PWAs most often rot: a cache-first SW serves your app from 2026 forever, and on iOS you can't easily force it. Also important: `api.github.com` and the tarball endpoint must be network-only — an SW that caches an API response will hand you a stale ETag and silently break sync.

questions.question: What caching and update strategy should the single root service worker use?

options.label: Precache shell, SWR, prompt to reload (Recommended)
options.description: Instant cold start offline, fresh code within one launch. A version constant names the cache; the new SW waits, the UI shows 'new version — reload', and skipWaiting runs on your tap so you are never upgraded mid-edit. GitHub API requests bypass the SW entirely.
options.preview:
const V = '2026-11-18.1';
install -> precache shell:
  /, /manifest.json, /shared/*.js,
  /calendar/, /calendar/app.js,
  icons, /shared/vendor/*

fetch:
  api.github.com | codeload
     -> fetch(), never cached
  same-origin -> cache, revalidate
     in background

new SW waiting -> banner
  'Update ready - reload'
  tap -> skipWaiting + reload

~40 lines, no staleness trap

options.label: Network-first, cache as fallback
options.description: Always try the network for app files and fall back to cache when offline. Can never be stale and needs no update prompt or version juggling at all. Cost: every launch waits on the network for the shell, so a weak signal means a slow start rather than an instant one.
options.preview:
fetch: try network
  ok      -> use + store
  fail    -> serve from cache

no versions, no prompt, no skipWaiting
~15 lines
slow launch on bad signal
(the common phone case)

options.label: Cache-first with manual version bump
options.description: Fastest possible launch, simplest mental model: serve from cache, only fetch on a cache miss, bump the version constant when you deploy. Cost: forget the bump and your phone runs last month's app indefinitely with no way to notice.
options.preview:
fetch: cache.match() || fetch()

fastest start
stale until you remember the bump
hard to recover from on iOS

content.text: Dependencies, which the CSP decision now constrains: no CDNs, so anything we use gets committed into `/shared/vendor/` and precached. Two parsers are in play — frontmatter YAML and RRULE expansion. Both are places where "it's only 80 lines" is how you get silent data corruption years later: YAML because you'll hand-edit these files in vim and expect real YAML to work, RRULE because `FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR` and DST-crossing weeklies are genuinely hard.

options.label: Vendor js-yaml + rrule.js (Recommended)
options.description: Both parsers are battle-tested, pinned by hand in /shared/vendor/, precached once by the SW. Hand-edited files always parse, and full RRULE works on read even though the UI only writes the easy cases. Cost: ~120 KB of vendored code you update manually, which for files you intend to keep for decades is the right trade.

Main app home screen. Two things to settle at once: a static host can't list directories, so the app list has to be declared somewhere; and in the reminders decision I leaned on "opening the app is the reminder", which only works if the root screen actually shows something.

content.text:
Last branch. Before writing anything down, one risk I should name rather than bury: `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/tarball/{ref}` 302-redirects to `codeload.github.com`, and I'm not certain codeload sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for authenticated private-repo downloads. If it doesn't, the tarball bootstrap fails in the browser and falls back to per-file fetching. That's a 20-minute spike, and it's the only decision above that could be invalidated by reality.

Two other unverified assumptions worth the same treatment: that an installed iOS PWA at `/mine/` really does share IndexedDB across `/mine/calendar/`, and that `{type:'module'}` service workers work on your iOS version.

# Mine

Mine is a set of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) to digitalize ones personal or professional life.
The key idea is to save everything in a repo as markdown files. This can be calendar entries, diaries, markdowns extracted from voice recordings / pdfs / .. These .md files can easily be ported to new apps without a vendor lock-in and are processed via an (AI) assistant to help you plan your day, keep track of tasks, remind you of memories a.k.a. a second brain.
To keep complexity to a minimum each use-case lives in a separate folder. e.g. the calendar PWA lives completely in a 'calendar' folder as does the zettelkasten and all the other apps. Each folder contains a 'sample' folder with samples how the markdowns shall look and a REQUIREMENTS.md to describe how the PWA works.

## Two repositories

| Repo | Visibility | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maximilianharr/mine` | public | this app, served by GitHub Pages at `/mine/` |
| `maximilianharr/mine-data` | **private** | the markdown data: `calendar/`, `zettelkasten/`, ... |

The app repo must be public because GitHub Pages cannot serve a private repo without
GitHub Enterprise. Data therefore never lives in this repo — it would be world-readable
at a predictable URL. The token the app holds is scoped to the data repo only, so a
leaked token cannot modify the app itself.

## One installable app, folders are routes

Mine is **one** PWA, not one PWA per folder. There is a single `manifest.json` with
`scope: /mine/` and a single service worker at the root. Subfolders are ordinary pages
inside that scope, reached by navigation.

This is what makes "set the token once" work: `/mine/` and `/mine/calendar/` are the
same origin, so they share one IndexedDB automatically, with no message passing. If each
folder were installed as its own home-screen app, iOS would give each one an isolated
storage container and the token would have to be entered again per app.

### Layout

```
/index.html            tile screen
/manifest.json         scope and start_url: /mine/
/sw.js                 one service worker, root scope, type: module
/shared/
  apps.js              APPS list - single source of truth
  store.js             IndexedDB: settings + file cache + sync queue
  github.js            GitHub API: bootstrap, pull, drain
  md.js                frontmatter parse / serialize
  vendor/              pinned third-party code, see VENDOR.md
/calendar/
  index.html
  app.js               imports ../shared/*.js by relative path
  widget.js            optional, exports summary()
  icon.svg
  REQUIREMENTS.md
  sample/
```

No build step. No bundler, no node_modules, no CI. `git push` is the deploy, and every
page can be opened directly from disk. All paths are relative, so the `/mine/` prefix
needs no configuration.

### Tile screen

`shared/apps.js` exports the list of apps and is imported by both the tile screen and
the service worker's precache list, so adding an app means editing one array.

Each tile shows the app's `icon.svg` above its folder name. An app may additionally ship
a `widget.js` exporting `summary()`; whatever it returns is rendered above the tiles.
The calendar's widget shows today's entries and the next one. This is deliberate: see
*Alerts* below — opening the app is the only reminder mechanism that works.

## PWA Setup & GitHub Sync

### Initialization (first run)

- User opens the main app URL (GitHub Pages) on the phone.
- User installs it via "Add to Home Screen" (iOS: Safari -> Share; Android: Chrome menu).
- On first launch, the app shows a setup screen asking for:
  - GitHub owner, **data** repo, and branch
  - Fine-grained personal access token, scoped to that one repo, "Contents: read and
    write", with an expiry date
- App checks the connection with a test request (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}`); on failure
  it shows a clear error naming the failing step.
- Settings and token are stored in IndexedDB. The expiry date is stored alongside, and
  the app warns 14 days before the token lapses. The token is never logged or displayed
  after entry.
- Service worker caches the app shell so the app opens offline.

### Token handling

The token is stored in plaintext in IndexedDB: it is as safe as the unlocked device. The
threat that matters is not a stolen phone but injected script on our own origin, which is
closed off by policy rather than encryption:

- Every page sends a strict CSP:
  `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://api.github.com https://codeload.github.com`
- **No CDNs, ever.** Every dependency is committed to `/shared/vendor/` and pinned by
  hand, with its source URL and version recorded in `VENDOR.md`. No unpkg, no cdnjs,
  no Google Fonts.
- The token is never written to a log, a URL, or the DOM.

### Cache model

Each app folder is mirrored locally in full. A decade of calendar entries is roughly
3000 files of ~500 B, so mirroring costs less than range-tracking logic and makes every
date available offline and search local and instant.

**Bootstrap** (first open of an app, 2 requests):

1. `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/tarball/{branch}` — the whole tree in one request. Decompressed
   with the native `DecompressionStream('gzip')`; the tar walk is ~40 lines.
2. `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/git/trees/{branch}?recursive=1` — all paths with their blob SHAs.

Only the opened app's folder is kept. Blob SHAs are stored per path; they are what later
pulls diff against and what writes send as their expected base.

**Pull** (on app open and on window focus):

1. `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/commits/{branch}` with `If-None-Match`. A `304` means nothing
   changed and costs no rate-limit quota.
2. On `200`: fetch the tree, diff blob SHAs against the cache, and fetch only the files
   whose SHA changed. Deleted paths are dropped from the cache.

### Sending data to GitHub

- User creates, edits, moves or deletes an item.
- The change is written to the local cache immediately (UI updates instantly) and appended
  to a sync queue. Each queued change records the blob SHA it was based on.
- The sync worker drains the whole queue as **one atomic commit** via the Git Data API:
  - `POST /git/blobs` per changed file
  - `POST /git/trees` with `base_tree` set to the current tree, listing additions and
    deletions (a deletion is an entry with `sha: null`)
  - `POST /git/commits`
  - `PATCH /git/refs/heads/{branch}` with the expected old SHA and **no force**
- One drain is one commit, so moving an entry — a delete plus a create, because the date
  is part of the path and the API has no rename — can never be half-applied, and a
  20-item offline backlog is one commit rather than twenty.
- If the ref update is rejected, someone pushed from elsewhere: pull, rebuild the tree on
  the new base, and retry. This succeeds, because almost every write in Mine is a create
  at a freshly generated path and cannot collide.
- **True conflict** — a queued change whose recorded base SHA no longer matches the remote
  blob at that path — means the same entry was edited in two places. Nothing is discarded:
  the remote version keeps the canonical path, and the local version is committed beside it
  as `<name>.conflict-<yyyymmdd>.md` with a `conflictOf:` key naming the original. The UI
  shows a banner offering keep mine / keep theirs / keep both. The leftover is plain
  markdown, readable in any editor and visible on every device. The queue never jams.

- Offline: the queue persists in IndexedDB and drains automatically when connectivity
  returns or the app is reopened.
- A sync indicator shows: in sync / pending / error.

Note that GitHub's Background Sync API does not exist in Safari, so draining happens in
the foreground, whenever the app is open.

### Service worker

- One service worker at the root, registered with `{type: 'module'}` so it can import the
  same `shared/apps.js` the tile screen uses.
- A version constant names the cache. On install the shell is precached: every page,
  every `shared/` module, `vendor/`, the icons and the manifest.
- Same-origin requests are served from cache and revalidated in the background.
- Requests to `api.github.com` and `codeload.github.com` **bypass the service worker
  entirely**. Caching an API response would hand back a stale ETag and silently break
  sync.
- A new service worker waits rather than activating. The UI shows an "Update ready —
  reload" banner, and `skipWaiting()` runs only on the user's tap, so an upgrade never
  lands mid-edit.

### Alerts

**No browser can schedule a local notification for a time when the app is closed.** The
Notification Triggers API was an origin trial that never shipped, and Periodic Background
Sync does not exist in Safari. Web Push would work, but something must be awake to send
it, which means a scheduler holding a token off-device.

For this reason, in v1:

- `alerts:` is stored and exported (it is valid `VALARM` data for `.ics`), but nothing
  fires in the background. Mine will not remind you while it is closed, and the
  requirements say so rather than implying otherwise.
- While the app is open, due alerts fire as real `Notification`s via `setTimeout`.
- The tile screen's calendar widget shows today and what is next, so opening the app is
  the reminder.

If background reminders are wanted later, the cheapest path that keeps data in these two
repos is a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow in the data repo sending Web Push with VAPID
keys held as repo secrets — accepting that GitHub cron drifts 5–20 minutes.

### Dependencies

Vendored into `/shared/vendor/`, pinned by hand:

| What | Why not hand-rolled |
| --- | --- |
| `js-yaml` | Files are hand-edited in an editor and must parse as real YAML — quoting, multiline scalars, flow maps. A subset parser misreads them silently. |
| `rrule` | `FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR` and DST-crossing weeklies are where hand-rolled expansion is wrong without telling you. |

YAML *writing* is ours (~20 lines): we control the output shape, so no dumper is needed.

## Spikes — unverified assumptions

Each of these is cheap to test and each has a documented fallback. They should be proven
on the actual target device before the code depending on them grows.

1. **codeload CORS.** `GET /tarball/{ref}` 302-redirects to `codeload.github.com`. If
   that host does not send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for an authenticated private-repo
   download, the browser fetch fails after the redirect.
   *Fallback:* bootstrap by walking the tree and fetching each blob individually — fine
   at today's file counts, degrading over the years.
2. **iOS shared storage.** That an installed PWA at `/mine/` really does share one
   IndexedDB with `/mine/calendar/` on the target iOS version.
   *Fallback:* none that is pleasant — this assumption is load-bearing for the whole
   "set the token once" design, so test it first.
3. **Module service workers.** `{type: 'module'}` requires Safari 16.4+.
   *Fallback:* a classic service worker with the app list duplicated in `sw.js`.

+Calendar is an app of [Mine](../REQUIREMENTS.md) to manage your calendar. It stores one
+entry per markdown file in the data repo and holds no state of its own beyond the shared
+cache described in the root requirements.
-Features
+## Data model
+### Paths
+calendar/2026/04/2026-04-18-1400-k3f9.md     one-off entry
+calendar/2026/04/2026-04-25-0000-ov1q.md     occurrence override
+calendar/recurring/trash-p7qm.md             entry with a recurrence rule
+calendar/groups.md                           group -> colour mapping
+The date lives in the path, so the Trees API listing alone tells the app which days have
+entries, before any file content is downloaded. The `-k3f9` suffix is 4 random characters,
+**not** a counter: two devices creating entries offline on the same day must never mint
+the same name. No title slug is used, so editing a title is never a rename.
+Entries carrying a `recurrence:` rule live in `calendar/recurring/` instead of the date
+tree, because an open-ended rule must render in months it was not created in. That folder
+stays small (tens of files) and is always cached; a view is that month's folder plus every
+rule expanded in memory over the visible range.
+### Frontmatter
+Keys follow RFC 5545 (iCalendar) naming where one exists, so `.ics` export is close to a
+field copy. **Empty keys are omitted, never written as `None`** — `None` is a YAML string,
+not null, and a parser hands it back as the text `"None"`.
+| Key | Applies to | Notes |
+| `title` | both | required |
+| `type` | both | `event` or `task` |
+| `start` | both | `DTSTART`. A bare date (`2026-04-18`) is all-day; a timestamp (`2026-04-18T14:00:00Z`) is an instant |
+| `end` | both | same value types as `start`; omitted for all-day single-day items |
+| `group` | both | a name, resolved through `groups.md` |
+| `done` | `task` only | `true` / `false` |
+| `location` | both | free text |
+| `alerts` | both | list of minutes before start; `0` means at start. Stored and exported only — see *Alerts* in the root requirements |
+| `participants` | both | list of email addresses |
+| `recurrence` | both | an RFC 5545 RRULE string, e.g. `FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA` |
+| `exdate` | recurring | occurrences to skip |
+| `rdate` | recurring | extra occurrences outside the rule |
+| `series` | override | the id of the recurring file it belongs to |
+| `recurrence-id` | override | `RECURRENCE-ID`: the original occurrence date this file replaces |
+| `conflictOf` | conflict file | written by sync, see root requirements |
+There is no `duration` key — it is `end - start`.

+the wrong day for anyone not on UTC, and breaks twice a year on DST.
+The markdown body below the frontmatter is the entry's content — an agenda, a checklist,
+notes. It is preserved byte-for-byte by anything that does not explicitly edit it.

+ticking it done, moving it, retitling it, cancelling it — is written as an **override

+rewritten, and because each override is a fresh path it can never conflict, even when

Both requirements files are rewritten and the samples now mirror the real data-repo layout. Nothing committed — that's yours.

**Answers to your two questions:**

Yes, the shared token works — and for a boring reason that's worth knowing: `/mine/` and `/mine/calendar/` are one origin, so one IndexedDB, no plumbing. The condition is that it stays **one installed PWA** with folders as routes. Install the calendar separately and iOS isolates its storage.

The REQUIREMENTS mostly made sense — the sync chapter was the right shape already. Seven things were wrong or missing, all now fixed:

| Was | Now |
| --- | --- |
| No repo split | public `mine` (Pages) + private `mine-data`; token scoped to data only |
| `alerts` implied working reminders | stated plainly: **nothing fires while closed**, no API exists; widget on the tile screen is the reminder |
| Samples disagreed (`start:`/`date:`, `done: None`) | one schema, RFC 5545 naming, `None` banned, bare date = all-day |
| `repeat: weekly` unanswerable | your `recurrence:` RRULE, in `recurring/`, with override files per occurrence |
| `20260418-1.md` counter | 4 random chars — two offline devices can't collide |
| Conflict = discard your edit | remote keeps the path, yours lands beside it as `.conflict-*.md` |
| Contents API, non-atomic moves | Git Data API, one commit per drain |

Three things I changed my mind on while costing them out, so you don't inherit my first answer: the "fetch *all* markdown" clause you wrote was right and my lazy-loading objection was wrong (1.5 MB after a decade); the tarball bootstrap replaces 3000 requests with 1; and your `BYDAY=SA` trash task is what settles "workdays" → 7 columns.

**Before writing code, three assumptions need 20 minutes on your actual phone** — documented as spikes with fallbacks at the end of `REQUIREMENTS.md`. The load-bearing one is #2: if an installed iOS PWA doesn't share IndexedDB across `/mine/calendar/`, the premise of your whole question fails and there's no pleasant fallback. #1 (does `codeload.github.com` send CORS headers for authenticated private downloads?) I genuinely don't know — it only costs you the tarball optimisation.
